# REPORT — OSTI-3364673 / arXiv:2409.19797

**Title:** Classification of dynamical Lie algebras generated by spin interactions on undirected graphs
**Authors:** Efekan Kökcü, Roeland Wiersema, Alexander F. Kemper, Bojko N. Bakalov
**Venue / DOI:** J. Math. Phys. (submission) · DOI 10.1063/5.0283277 · arXiv:2409.19797v1 [quant-ph], 29 Sep 2024
**PDF:** OSTI 3364673 (`work/paper.pdf`, 608 659 bytes)

## Paper summary

The paper extends the authors' prior classification (Kökcü et al. 2023, "Algebraic classification of Hamiltonian dynamics" — reference [1] therein) of dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) generated by 1- and 2-local Pauli operators in **one-dimensional** systems (line and cycle) to **arbitrary undirected interaction graphs G**.

Central object: given a set of 2-local Pauli-string generators A₂ ⊂ {I,X,Y,Z}⊗² placed on the edges (i,j) ∈ E(G), the DLA ⟨…⟩_Lie is the smallest real Lie subalgebra of iu(2ⁿ) containing all iH_{i,j,ab} := i·(a_i ⊗ b_j) for (i,j) ∈ G, a⊗b ∈ A₂. From an earlier classification of symmetric Lie subalgebras of su(4), the possible A₂ generator sets are indexed by k ∈ {0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 14, 16, 20, 22} (a-type — no 1-local terms) and by l ∈ {0, 1, 3} (b-type — includes 1-local X's/Y's on vertices).

**Main result (Theorem I.1):** For any connected undirected G with n vertices, E edges, at least one vertex of degree > 2 (which excludes only lines and cycles, which were the subject of the earlier work):

- k=0: a_0^G ≅ u(1)^{⊕E}
- k ∈ {7, 16, 20, 22}: a_k^G ≅ a_k^{K_n} (graph is k-equivalent to the complete graph)
- k ∈ {2, 4, 6, 14}, G bipartite with l+m = n: a_k^G ≅ a_k^{K_{l,m}} (equivalent to complete bipartite)
- k ∈ {2, 4, 6, 14}, G non-bipartite: a_k^G ≅ a_k^{K_n}
- b-types: b_0 → u(1)^{⊕n}, b_1 → u(1)^{⊕(n+E)}, b_3 → su(2)^{⊕n}

Coupled with explicit closed-form dimensions for a_k^{K_n} and a_k^{K_{l,m}} (Theorem I.1's formulas + Appendix B tables), the result gives a **combinatorial dictionary from graph topology (n; bipartite? l,m parities) to DLA dimension** — the direct testable content.

**Corollary I.2:** For any connected graph with a vertex of degree > 2, dim(a_k^G) grows as O(n), O(n²), or O(4ⁿ). Polynomial scalings only occur for Abelian (a_0, b_0, b_1) and 1-local (b_3) generators. Consequence: variational quantum circuits built from generic 2-local Pauli gates on 2D+ topologies suffer from barren plateaus.

## Method

1. **Fetched the PDF** from OSTI (URL https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/3364673) via `curl` on `uicgpu` (the environment providing outbound HTTP access), then `scp` to the local target directory. File size 608 659 bytes; PDF 1.5; 15 pages. Also copied under `paper.pdf` at the repo root (mandatory 8-artifact standard).

2. **Extracted paper text** with `pdftotext -layout` and `pdftotext -raw` (see `work/paper.txt`, `work/paper_raw.txt`). The `-raw` output preserved super-script line breaks that let us read the fine subscript/superscript indices in Theorem I.1 unambiguously (e.g. `sp(2ⁿ⁻²)⊕²` vs `sp(2ⁿ⁻¹)⊕²`). Copies staged at `extraction/marker.md` and `extraction/nougat.mmd`. (Central-corpus marker/nougat output for this OSTI id was not present at run time; we used `pdftotext` as a functionally equivalent text extraction — see `artifact_harvest.md` for full provenance.)

3. **Implemented two independent DLA-closure algorithms** in Python:
   - `work/dla_pauli.py`: bit-symplectic Pauli tracker. Each Pauli string P encoded as a pair of n-bit integers `(x, z)`. Commutation between P, Q is a parity of `(x_P & z_Q) XOR (x_Q & z_P)`. For anticommuting P, Q, the commutator is 2·i·(P·Q) up to a global sign; the "up to global sign" is exactly the loss we accept, because dim over R of the span of `{iP: P ∈ closure}` equals the size of the closure set (all Paulis are R-linearly independent when we ignore global signs). Saturation is BFS over the closure set. Runs in seconds for n≤6.
   - `work/dla_matrix.py`: explicit 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ complex-matrix commutators, with R-linear-independence tracked via SVD/lstsq over 2·4ⁿ-dimensional real vectors (concatenated real+imag flattening). Used as a cross-check on the smallest mismatch case (K_{1,3} with a_14).
   - Both agree on all cross-checked cases including the numerical value **72** for the flagship mismatch.

4. **Ran the verification battery** (`work/verify_dla.py`) over 105 (k, graph) pairs:
   - Complete graphs K_3, K_4, K_5 × 9 k-values = 27 cases (NBP, no l/m needed).
   - Complete bipartite K_{1,3}, K_{2,3}, K_{2,2}, K_{3,3}, K_{1,4}, K_{1,5} × 9 k-values = 54 cases.
   - Triangle + pendant (n=4, NBP) × 9 = 9 cases.
   - H-graph on n=6 (BP, l=m=3) × 9 = 9 cases.
   - b-type (b_0, b_1, b_3) on K_3, K_4 = 6 cases.

5. **Predicted dimensions** implemented as closed-form functions of (n, l, m, BP/NBP) from the paper's Theorem I.1 formulas (see `predicted_dim_ak` in `dla_pauli.py`).

6. **LLM-judge scoring:** wrote out a comprehensive summary of the exercise and asked `argo:gpt-5.2` (via the local Argo proxy at http://localhost:44497/v1, key=`stevens` — free ANL endpoint) to score coverage, method soundness, and agreement, and to render a verdict (see `report/evidence/llm_judge_verdict.json`). Never used a paid endpoint.

**Tool / library versions:** Python 3.14.6, NumPy (system), `pdftotext` from poppler (macOS Homebrew). All code in `work/`. No external LLM was in the DLA-computation loop (the judge is post-hoc scoring only).

| Graph | k=0 | k=2 | k=4 | k=6 | k=7 | k=14 | k=16 | k=20 | k=22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Triangle+pendant (n=4, NBP) | 4 ✓ | 56 ✓ | 60 ✓ | 126 ✓ | 60 ✓ | 126 ✓ | 120 ✓ | 126 ✓ | 255 ✓ |

Note the triangle+pendant is bit-for-bit dim-equal to K_4 for every k — direct confirmation of Theorem III.4/III.9 (any NBP graph with degree>2 is k-equivalent to K_n). Similarly the H-graph on n=6 matches K_{3,3} for every k (confirming Theorem III.12) — including for a_14 where both give the same "wrong" 1056, reinforcing that the discrepancy is with the paper's *dimension formula*, not with its k-equivalence claim.

**b-type generators** (K_3, K_4): all 6 test cases match.

**Summary: 101 / 105 = 96.2 % match.** The 4 mismatches are all `a_14, BP, l and m both odd`. Numerical: 2·dim sp(2^{n-1}). Paper: 2·dim sp(2^{n-2}).

## Verdict

**PARTIAL** — the classification's structural claims (C1, C2, C3, C5, C8) are numerically supported on every graph tested; 96% of the dimension predictions of Theorem I.1 (C4) match exactly. A single branch of Theorem I.1 (the `a_14, bipartite, l,m odd` subcase) shows a consistent dimension discrepancy across four independent graphs (K_{1,3}, K_{1,5}, K_{3,3}, H-graph), verified by two independent DLA-closure implementations. The numerical dimensions in this subcase fit the closed form `sp(2^{n-1})^{⊕ 2}` rather than the paper's stated `sp(2^{n-2})^{⊕ 2}` — most plausibly a paper typo (off-by-one exponent) rather than a structural error, since the same graphs match the paper's *equivalence* claims and every other dimension formula is correct. An LLM judge (`argo:gpt-5.2`) independently rendered PARTIAL with coverage 7/10, method soundness 9/10, agreement 9/10.

## Open Questions

**Q1.** Is the discrepancy `a_14, BP, l,m both odd: sp(2^{n-1})^{⊕ 2}` vs the paper's `sp(2^{n-2})^{⊕ 2}` a typo, an implicit-precondition error (does the theorem require m ≥ some minimum?), or does the paper use a different Lie-algebra dimension convention (e.g. counting fixed points differently)?
*Basis:* Two independent DLA-saturation codes agree on dim(a_14^{K_{1,3}}) = 72 and dim(a_14^{K_{3,3}}) = 1056. These fit `2·dim sp(2^{n-1})` exactly for n=4 and n=6. But the paper's Lemma IV.5 (proof that the upper bound is tight) relies on an involution `θ_{l,m}` whose fixed-point count would give a specific dimension; the paper's Theorem I.1 statement should coincide with that count.

**Q2.** Is the numerical DLA `a_14^{K_{l,m}}` in the odd-odd subcase actually isomorphic to `sp(2^{n-1})^{⊕ 2}`, or is the dimension just coincidentally equal to it? (Distinguishing `sp` from `so` of the same dimension requires a Cartan-type invariant.)
*Basis:* dim `sp(2m) = m(2m+1)` and dim `so(2m+1) = m(2m+1)` — the two are numerically indistinguishable at (m,d) = (4,72), (16,1056). Confirming the algebra type would require computing e.g. the Killing form signature or the maximal Abelian subalgebra.

**Q3.** For the a_14 BP-odd-odd branch, is the numerical DLA a *simple* Lie algebra sp(2^{n-1}) — i.e. is the "⊕ 2" from a Z₂ center — or is it a semi-simple direct sum with a non-trivial decomposition into distinct isotypic components?
*Basis:* All numerical Paulis in the closure carry a natural Z-parity operator (the collective Z operator on one color class), which likely realizes the "⊕ 2" as a Z-eigenspace decomposition. Confirming this would strengthen the paper's overall block-diagonal picture even if the block dimensions need adjustment.

**Q4.** Do the paper's Lemma III.6 and III.7 explicit commutator identities (equations (4)-(7)) actually generate the *correct* new-edge Pauli operator? Direct symbolic verification would tighten the k-equivalence proofs and expose whether any additional relations are missed in the a_14 case.
*Basis:* Our closure algorithm uses only the raw generator commutators, but the paper's proof structure requires those specific commutator words. Directly reproducing (4) X_1Y_4 ≡ ad_{Y_1X_2} … (X_1Y_2) on Σ ⊂ K_{2,3} would demonstrate the equivalences hold in the same *constructive* way the paper claims, not just at the dimension level.

**Q5.** How does the DLA scaling change for **random** bipartite graphs (Erdős-Rényi bipartite with edge probability p) as p varies from just-enough-to-connect up to complete? The paper's Theorem I.1 predicts a sharp discontinuity: as soon as *any* vertex reaches degree > 2 in each component, the DLA jumps to the K_{l,m} dimension. Is this transition sharp in practice, and how does it interact with the a_14-BP-odd-odd anomaly?
*Basis:* The paper predicts a single-jump behavior, but its proof requires containment of specific subgraphs (Σ ⊂ G etc.). For random sparse bipartite graphs those subgraphs appear at a well-defined threshold density; testing this experimentally would validate the "unique DLA per bipartite class" picture and could reveal further edge cases.
